China and the US can and must develop and manage AI “for good”, Chinese leader Xi Jinping has told Donald Trump , further ramping up tensions with the American president who has dubbed fears over the technology “a hoax”.
On his first state visit to the US in more than a decade, Mr Xi told Mr Trump: “Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence. [We must] ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people.”
The US president had rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese leader amid friction between the two superpowers, largely over global trade.
Thursday's lavish ⁠state summit at the White House appeared heavy on symbolism but light on substance, with no sign of major breakthroughs between the world's biggest economies, even as Mr Trump highlighted progress under a bilateral trade mechanism.
Both leaders also identified AI as an area of cooperation.
AI bosses have sounded the alarm in recent weeks over the potential of the technology to threaten the future of the human race. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI maker ChatGPT, said the world was right to be afraid of AI, and the warnings have led to new calls for regulation of the technology.
But at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Mr Trump dismissed calls for stricter controls, branding the warnings “a hoax”, setting up a clash with the Chinese leader. He also said he wanted AI to be renamed “super-intelligence”.
Mr Xi’s visit began in Washington on Thursday with much fanfare, including a military ceremony, a flyover at the Rose Garden and Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof.
However, the meeting between the leaders of the world’s two largest economies comes as Mr Trump faces international backlash for inviting Russian president Vladimir Putin to Miami’s G20 gathering in December despite the war in Ukraine.
Mr Trump, who has dubbed his relationship with Mr Xi the “G2”, said their meeting would have an impact on the world for decades to come.
“During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and 'super-intelligence’,” Mr Trump said.
“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.”
Mr Xi was treated to a state dinner on Thursday evening with tech executives including Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Open AI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai.
But analysts cautioned that the intense competition between the two countries in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements.
Mr Xi used his initial address to emphasise that the US has the “capability and responsibility to manage AI for good”.
“ China -US cooperation may not solve every problem in the world, but without our cooperation, it would be hard to solve many of the world's problems,” he said.
He voiced hope for a more stable relationship with the US, saying Beijing and Washington should be “partners, not rivals” and that the “historical logic of peaceful coexistence” between the two countries had not changed.
The two are expected to discuss the ongoing Iran war but there has been little sign China is willing to exert pressure on its ally to yield to US demands.
Mr Trump has been warned about the relationship between Tehran and Beijing as the war he started in February continues with no end in sight.
“The president needs to tell Xi Jinping that this is a dangerous alliance,” Jonathan Schanzer, executive director of the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, told Fox News before the visit.
“The Chinese assistance to the Iranian regime has actually expanded on a number of fronts,” he warned, citing the provision of drone parts and motors, dual use chemicals, alleged assistance with targeting and an economic relationship.
Disputes over Taiwan remained the most contentious issue as China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own. Mr Xi is keen to press Mr Trump to halt arms sales to the democratically governed island.
As expected, the Chinese president pressed Mr Trump on Taiwan on Thursday, saying he hoped the US would "handle the Taiwan question with prudence."
After his May summit with Mr Xi, MrTrump, whose administration in December approved an $11bn arms sale package to Taiwan, said he was holding a second package, worth some $14bn, in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip".
Craig Singleton of the Foundation for Defense of ‌Democracies think tank said Beijing may believe it has established a new baseline on Taiwan with Mr Trump.
Mr Xi's use ​of the word "adhere" was revealing because "it implies Beijing believes Washington is already behaving in ways it wants”, he told the Associated Press.
"In the ‌context of the current stand-down on Taiwan arms sales, China ⁠may increasingly view that restraint as a new baseline rather than a temporary pause," he said.
"Beijing's objective is ⁠to get Trump to absorb Chinese red lines into his own definition of a stable relationship."
Sources told Reuters said that Beijing is offering to help put pressure on Iran in return.
After their previous meeting earlier this year, Mr Trump had said he was holding in abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth $14 billion and called it a “very good negotiating chip”.
Mr Trump, known to be impressed with ceremony and symbolic gestures, has attempted to reciprocate the grand welcome he received when he made his own state visit to China in May.
On Wednesday evening he greeted Mr Xi with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews – the first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader in that manner since President Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015.
The Chinese leader’s visit comes at the end of busy week for international diplomacy in the US, with the UN General Assembly still taking place in New York.
Secretary of state Marco Rubio announced the Putin invite after meeting Russia’s outspoken foreign secretary Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the event Wednesday, and soon faced international backlash.
“It's clearly, I think, the wrong path to normalise people who are starting wars, who are going against the UN charter, who are killing and giving orders to kill civilians,” the EU’s representative for foreign affairs Kaja Kallas told Sky News in response .
The European Commission also issued thinly veiled criticism of the US invitation.
“Russia is escalating attacks on Ukrainian civilians as we speak. July and August were the deadliest months since the war started,” deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill said.
“Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion and to call for it to end.
“What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”
The state dinner wrapped up with Mr Xi saying that the two leaders shared a “sincere and indepth exchange”.
Mr Trump will take the Chinese leader on Friday to the US National archives. They would also see "artefacts testifying to the long and cherished relationship" between China and the US and their "cultural exchanges,” he said in remarks welcoming Mr Xi.

Donald Trump couldn’t help but offer guests at his state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping a first-ever tour of his ballroom construction site.
The president loves to boast to the White House press corps and his Truth Social followers about his passion projects around Washington, D.C ., especially the massive White House ballroom being built. Now, in front of an international audience, Trump has offered to share a glimpse of what he called a “clean and sparkly” construction site.
“And if I could go off script just for a second,” Trump said as dinner guests in the East Room of the White House laughed. “But as a special treat in honor of President Xi and Madame [Liyuan] Peng. I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back.”
“It's one year away from completion — the new ballroom that you've heard about, and you will see something that I think you will really love.”
The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom will fit 650 seats, compared to the 200 seats in the East Room. Trump has said construction will cost about $400 million and that he and other donors would pay for it.
But the project’s contractor told the administration that it would cost $600 million , with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.
The Trump administration has also been challenged in court over whether it had the authority to tear down the East Wing last October to build the ballroom without Congressional approval. The Supreme Court ruled last month that the president can continue with construction for the time being .
“You'll be the first people to step foot on that, and we'll do that maybe after we're finished with the entertainment tonight. Anybody [who] wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkly, it's our honor to have you do so,” Trump told his dinner guests.
The official delegations from the US and China attended the state dinner. Some notable names on the guest list included first lady Melania Trump , Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .
Trump was photographed next to Melania while waiting to greet Xi and his wife Peng at the White House ahead of the dinner. Makeup was caked on his left hand, which he often uses to cover up bruising .
The Trump administration has said the black and blue on the back of his hands is due to frequent handshaking and aspirin use .
Several of America’s tech leaders, such as SpaceX’s Elon Musk , OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg , were also in attendance Thursday night amid an AI race with China .
During the legal fight to build his ballroom, Trump argued that it was needed for national security. Underneath the East Wing sits a bunker dating back to 1942, after the U.S. entered World War II. In court filings, the Trump administration noted that bomb shelters, military installations and a medical facility would be added to the bunker during construction.
So when Trump suggested officials from China, an adversary of the U.S., tour the construction site, it raised some eyebrows.
“Of the security bunker? Seems suboptimal,” Reuters journalist Charlie Szymanski wrote on Bluesky.
“Guided tour of the super secure and classified military ballroom for officials of a foreign unfriendly nation. Totally reasonable,” another Bluesky user, Jeff Domingues, posted .
One X user wrote , “Let’s take the leader of China into the ballroom that doubles as a military bunker! Great idea Don!”
Melania led the preparations for the state dinner, which included a menu that the White House said had a “subtle Chinese influence.” For the main course, guests enjoyed sesame-crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy.
Entertainment for the night was headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s second inauguration. Guests were also treated to performances by military ensembles.
“Thank you, Mr. President and Mrs. Trump, for extending to my wife and me your gracious hospitality and thoughtful arrangements,” Xi said at the dinner through an interpreter. “You make us feel truly at home.”
“I would also like to extend my sincere greetings to Americans from all sectors of society who care about China-U.S. relations and support the further growth of our bilateral ties.”

President Donald Trump is taking Chinese President Xi Jinping to visit the National Archives on Friday, showing off the sacred texts of U.S. democracy to the leader of the world’s most powerful communist country to cap off a three-day state visit criticized for being heavy on pomp and light on substance.
While Trump warmly welcomed Xi to Washington , outside the White House , protests against Xi continued almost nonstop Thursday. The demonstrators represented a range of causes, from calls for religious autonomy and greater freedoms in Tibet, Hong Kong and the ethnic region of Xinjiang to demands to keep China out of self-governed Taiwan.
Xi’s day will begin at the White House
There, President Trump and first lady Melania Trump will host the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for tea.
Macron says a U.S. diesel ban would inflict economic damage across the world
On Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron said in an interview with French broadcasters that the diesel ban would damage economies across the world, including the U.S.
“This decision would be bad, not just for the rest of the world, but for the American economy, too,” Macron said. “I can tell you one thing: it wouldn’t be a good decision for his country and its economy.”
The European Union has increasingly turned to the U.S. for diesel since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the outbreak of the Iran war in February. The support Trump expressed this week for banning diesel exports to drive down U.S. prices worries the bloc, which would have to find alternative sources of the fuel.
Japan’s Takaichi says her country and the U.S. are allies
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, asked about Trump’s remark during his talks with China’s Xi Jinping that their countries were “allies” during World War II, said Japan and the United States are close allies of mutual trust today.
“Japan and the United States waged war but we have since firmly reconciled, deepened our relationship and now we trust each other as strongly bonded allies,” Takaichi said.
Japan worries about closer U.S.-China ties at a time Tokyo struggles to mend worsening ties with Beijing. Takaichi’s comment last year that a potential Chinese military action against Taiwan could justify Japanese involvement outraged Beijing, spilling over to trade.
Protesters of Xi’s policies push for change in earshot of White House visit with Trump
Trump warmly welcomed Chinese leader Xi Jinping with a personal airport greeting, a tour of his new helipad and a candlelit dinner. But outside the White House, protests against Xi continued almost nonstop Thursday during his state visit.
The demonstrators represented a range of causes, from calls for religious autonomy and greater freedoms in Tibet, Hong Kong and the ethnic region of Xinjiang to demands to keep China out of self-governed Taiwan.
Protests against visiting Chinese leaders are nothing new — in 2006, a woman heckled Xi’s predecessor Hu Jintao at a White House welcome ceremony — but Xi has become the focus of attacks for his tough approach to tightening control over Xinjiang, Hong Kong and other regions and the Chinese military’s growing threats to Taiwan, which he says must come under Chinese rule.
Crowds gathered behind a fence along Lafayette Park, waving flags and holding signs. Loudspeakers carried their voices across the park to the White House’s North Portico, where an honor guard and a red carpet awaited guests attending the state dinner.
Xi is wrapping his visit to Washington with a peek at the Constitution and Bill of Rights
Trump is taking Chinese President Xi Jinping to visit the National Archives on Friday, showing off the sacred texts of U.S. democracy to the leader of the world’s most powerful communist country to cap off a three-day state visit criticized for being heavy on pomp and light on substance.
Xi is expected to depart Washington after touring the nation’s vault of records, where the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights are held. The two leaders have made a show of working to preserve harmony between the world’s two largest economies, though there were no major breakthroughs on issues such as trade or the safety of artificial intelligence.
The visit comes as the U.S. celebrates the 250th anniversary of its founding, and Trump said Thursday that he wanted to show Xi “some of the greatest treasures of that proud history.”
The U.S. president also said he wanted to show Xi artifacts about the relationship between the two countries.

articles.title_orig: Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
articles.title_zh: Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
articles.content_orig:
Xi Jinping’s visit heavy on symbolism but no sign closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on thorny issues such as AI, trade, Taiwan and Iran
Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on AI, trade and a growing US-China strategic rivalry expected to feature on an elaborate state visit that critics say went big on style but lacked substance.
Here are the key takeaways from Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade.
Senate Democrats criticised Trump’s summit with Xi, saying it prioritised pageantry over substance on the major issues. There was no sign a brief closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on the thorny issues of AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran.
Both countries agreed to extend until 10 January an agreement pausing their trade war, but experts said there were few other obvious tangible outcomes.
Xi once again invoked the “Thucydides Trap” , an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one often results in war. Xi said the risk “can be overcome” and urged cooperation.
After their meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House’s South Lawn. “He loves good granite,” Trump told reporters, adding the two men had a “great meeting” ​without elaborating.
Danny Russel, a former US diplomat serving in the Obama administration, expressed concern that the two leaders spent more time on social and ceremonial events than the actual meeting, which was about 90 minutes.
“Pageantry and protocol don’t add up to progress. Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths,” said Russel. “What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as ‘diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the US-China relationship.”
AI analysts were forced to read between the lines to gauge the outcome of AI discussions between the pair.
Trump had written in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that he and Xi would discuss “super intelligence” (Trump’s newly coined term for AI) but suggested he had little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans.
“Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of ⁠discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.”
During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must “ensure that the development of AI is always ​under human control”.
Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for ​anything beyond symbolic agreements.
During ​the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary.
Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his visit to China in May , Trump said he was holding in ⁠abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth about $14bn and called it a “very good negotiating chip” – rattling some US allies in Asia.
In a statement signed by at least 19 ⁠of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, ​Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to ‌immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale.
China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island.
Trump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the ‌first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome.
For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags.
Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico .
Thursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang.
First lady Melania Trump’s menu featured yellow squash velouté, sesame-crusted sea bass and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit.
In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending . While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps.
Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

The 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Friday that states have a right to regulate sports-related event contracts on prediction market platforms, marking a second major legal defeat for the industry as a fight at the U.S. Supreme Court looms.
In a unanimous decision, the three judge panel said that Ohio and Tennessee are permitted to apply their state gambling laws to Kalshi's sports-related event contracts.
"We hold that Kalshi has not shown that its sports-event contracts satisfy the statutory definition of a 'swap' so as to fall within the scope of the CFTC's 'exclusive jurisdiction,'" the opinion said.
Kalshi and other prediction market platforms argue all event contracts are swaps , a type of financial derivative that is regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission . However, states assert that platforms' sports-related offerings amount to gambling , and thus should be regulated by their laws related to sports betting.
This disagreement has spawned a legal battle across the country as states sue platforms for operating what they often claim are illegal gambling operations, while exchanges also sue states to block them from enforcing local laws on what they argue should be federally-regulated financial exchanges.
The CFTC has sued nine states to defend what it believes is its exclusive right to regulate event contracts, given to it by the Commodity Exchange Act. But the 6th Circuit panel rejected that notion.
"Even assuming that Kalshi's sports-event contracts are swaps, we alternatively hold that the CEA neither expressly nor impliedly preempts Ohio's or Tennessee's gambling laws," the opinion said. The decision overturns a Tennessee federal district court ruling that sided with Kalshi, and reaffirms a decision by a federal district court in Ohio that sided with the states' argument.
"Kalshi attempted an end run around Tennessee law to avoid any of the rules or taxes associated with sports gambling. They failed," said Jonathan Skrmetti, Tennessee's attorney general.
"Sports wagering is heavily regulated because it can do a lot of harm, and I'm glad we thwarted Kalshi's efforts to remove every safeguard and put Tennessee sports bettors at risk," he added.
Kalshi nor the CFTC immediately responded to requests for comment. CNBC has also reached out to the Ohio attorney general's office for comments.
The latest ruling now means prediction market platforms have notched two losses in legal fights at the appeals court level. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled last month that Nevada has a right to regulate sports-related event contracts, stating that they were sports bets and not swaps. Meanwhile, the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against New Jersey in April and said the CFTC has the exclusive right to regulate all swaps, no matter the contract type.
New Jersey appealed that decision in a petition to the Supreme Court earlier this month. It is not clear whether the Supreme Court will take up the case now, or wait until further decisions from circuit courts on the issue of sports-related event contracts are delivered.

Donald Trump has attacked what he calls a “sick conspiracy” against AI after the head of Anthropic called for a slowdown in the technology’s development.
The US president warned that China would benefit after the bosses of Silicon Valley’s top AI companies backed calls to restrict AI development for safety reasons, calling the concerns a “hoax”.
He also launched a tirade against Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, whom he accused of trying to be a “perfect little angel”.
Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social: “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so!
“We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!
“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”
Mr Amodei released a letter at the weekend calling for an industry-wide slowdown, endorsed by the US government, to prevent safety issues going “seriously wrong”.
In response, Mr Trump wrote: “Concerning AI, when, in the history of business, did anyone see the leaders of an industry call for regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy.
“AI taking over the world, destroying humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX.”
JD Vance, the US vice-president, echoed Mr Trump’s comments, calling tech leaders’ requests a “Trojan horse”.
He added: “I have to say, just personally, I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them.
“It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse.”
OpenAI has since called on the UK Government to introduce mandatory safety rules for major AI developers.
Under proposals supported by the company, the UK’s AI Security Institute would play a central role in third-party testing and creating adaptive technical standards.
Tom Duff-Gordon, the company’s head of policy in Europe, the Middle East and Africa, told Politico: “OpenAI is in a position to support legislation in the UK to establish durable, mandatory, capability-based requirements for frontier AI that would build on the set of voluntary commitments that we currently have.”
Under the plans, Britain would move from the current system of voluntary agreements with AI companies to enforceable standards, bringing the UK in line with emerging frameworks in the EU and US.
The Government has not yet put forward plans for AI safety legislation, despite pressure from backbench MPs.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Wall Street after AI bosses called for a slowdown, with the Nasdaq Composite dropping by as much as 1.3pc.
Nvidia, the world’s largest listed company and a manufacturer of semiconductors used in the AI race, plunged by 4.2pc while fellow chipmaker AMD dropped 6.2pc.
The main European indexes in France, Germany and Spain were all down sharply on Monday after falls in South Korea and Japan overnight.

articles.title_orig: Trump warns Xi on support for Iran, receives assurances, US envoy says
articles.title_zh: Trump warns Xi on support for Iran, receives assurances, US envoy says
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump warned Chinese President Xi Jinping against providing support to Iran during talks in Washington, DC, this week and received assurances that China would not do so, the U.S. ambassador to China said Sept. 25.
The warning came amid reports that China had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.
David Perdue, Trump's ambassador to Beijing, said in a CNBC interview that Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was "totally unacceptable."
Asked separately on Fox News if that meant China would stop assisting Iran, Perdue said U.S. officials received assurances from Beijing on Sept. 24.
"We've seen movement ... on that already. That's what the commitment is. They assured us yesterday they're not doing that," Perdue told Fox News' "America's Newsroom" program.
Trump later on Sept. 25 acknowledged that the two leaders discussed the war that the United States and Israel launched on Iran in late February, without giving details.
U.S. lawmakers had urged Trump to confront Xi over reports of Chinese assistance to Iran, raising concerns that Chinese entities may have given targeting help that led to US casualties in the conflict.
Chinese officials have assured Iran that even after the Trump-Xi meeting China will not limit its economic, political or military ties with Tehran under pressure from the U.S. president, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Sept. 25.
Reuters reported in July that Iran was expected to receive within weeks a first shipment out of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers.
Iran has also used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter told Reuters earlier this month.
Chinese state newswire Xinhua reported on Sept. 24 that Xi had urged the United States and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran.
Trump and Xi did not take formal questions during the three-day state visit to Washington.
Earlier this month, Trump brushed aside a report ​that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three U.S. troops there in July.
"They basically do what we do," Trump ​told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sept. 13. "When they say China spies on us, I say ​you're right and we spy on them too."
(Reporting by Katharine Jackson, Susan Heavey, Bo Erickson and Parisa Hafezi; Additional reporting by Simon Lewis and David Brunnstrom; Editing by Peter Graff, Mark Porter, Chris Reese and Sanjeev Miglani)

articles.title_orig: Ed Sheeran shows at Gillette Stadium are canceled due to weather
articles.title_zh: Ed Sheeran shows at Gillette Stadium are canceled due to weather
articles.content_orig:
Ed Sheeran’s concerts scheduled for this weekend at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been canceled due to severe weather, amid wider turmoil surrounding the British pop star’s tour.
The concerts scheduled for Friday and Saturday at the New England Patriots home stadium were scrapped because of the upcoming nor’easter , Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” the statement said. “The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority.”
The touring group said that refunds are available and that ticket holders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded.
The announcement comes amid a wider scandal for Sheeran’s “Loop” tour since one of its opening acts was forced out for voicing pro-Palestinian views.
Earlier this month, rapper Macklemore said he was removed from Sheeran’s tour after speaking out in support for the Palestinian people at the tour’s shows in New Jersey. Macklemore said he was removed at the behest of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and alleged that Kraft organized a boycott among stadium owners.
Kraft did not immediately return a request for comment. In a previous statement he said he did not intend to stifle Palestinian support but to ensure a “welcoming environment” at Gillette Stadium.
Macklemore’s removal prompted Sheeran’s other opening acts — Aaron Rowe, Lukas Graham, Finneas and his house band, Beoga — to withdraw in protest.
A rep for Sheeran did not immediately return a request for comment. In his first concert since the scandal, Sheeran apologized for the scenario.
“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said, “but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”
On Thursday, Macklemore announced a Free Palestine Tour for this fall.
The multiday nor’easter is expected to hit the East Coast, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island. Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people. Wind gusts are expected to peak on Saturday, reaching up to 60 mph in coastal locations.
Sheeran’s shows weren’t the only major musical events canceled due to the threat of severe weather in the North East, with the Global Citizen Festival at Central Park in New York City also pulling the plug.
“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” the organization wrote on social media .
“Safety has to come first,” Global Citizen added, noting that this is the first time the festival has been canceled in 14 years.
All Things Go , another New York City festival that was to be held at Forrest Hills Stadium in Queens this weekend, was also canceled due to the weather.
And a Friday night concert at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey by Australian rock legends AC/DC was postponed just hours before the show.
I’m a reporter on NBC News’ breaking news team, covering crime, extreme weather, pop culture and more. I recently covered Hurricane Milton, which devastated the Tampa, Florida, metropolitan area, and the student-led protests at Columbia University.

The Supreme Court has temporarily unblocked a controversial federal voter database ahead of November's midterms, granting President Donald Trump a temporary legal victory in his push against noncitizen voting .
The court’s three liberal justices issued a public dissent against the decision.
The emergency order permits state officials, for the time being, to access the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, to check the eligibility of individuals on their voter rolls.
Participation in the SAVE initiative remains voluntary for states.
Its immediate effect on the coming midterms is likely limited because federal law prohibits states from conducting systematic purges of voter rolls within 90 days of an election, according to David Becker, an election law expert who leads the Center for Election Innovation and Research.
Becker noted that since participation is optional and DHS acknowledges its data is imperfect, "states may find this to be a useful tool used along with other tools to keep their lists up-to-date."
Friday's directive puts on hold a June decision by U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan, who had declared the Republican administration’s expanded version of SAVE illegal.
She had suspended access to the database, ruling that it infringed on privacy rights and presented a substantial risk of incorrectly disenfranchising eligible voters.
A federal appeals court had allowed her ruling to stand.
However, the Supreme Court majority concluded that a 1996 statute explicitly authorizes DHS to collect immigration and citizenship records from federal agencies, adding that the federal government is under "an obligation to respond" when states request citizenship verification.
"The order below prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task," the majority stated in an unsigned order.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson authored the dissent, joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor.
She highlighted that the database has long been understood to fall under federal privacy laws and warned of significant risks that valid voter registrations could be improperly revoked.
"The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," Jackson wrote.
Legal representatives for the plaintiffs characterized the decision as "profoundly disappointing," warning that it leaves "millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database" ahead of the midterms.
"However, this case is not over," the group declared in a statement. "The D.C. district court ruled that the expanded SAVE program violated multiple laws. We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans’ voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands."
The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Created under immigration law to help state and local entities restrict government benefits to noncitizens, the SAVE program's search capabilities were broadened by the Trump administration last year.
Since that expansion, at least 67 million voter records have been scanned, raising concerns among critics about accidental purges of legal voters.
Errors have already been documented. Officials in Travis County, Texas, reported reviewing 97 voters flagged as noncitizens by SAVE, discovering that between 10% and 21% were actually U.S. citizens.
The county asked the Supreme Court to reject the administration's appeal, whereas the state of Texas submitted a brief supporting the database.
Despite the injunction against SAVE over recent months, court filings reveal the administration continued utilizing Social Security Administration records "in certain cases to verify information and help determine whether illegal voting may have occurred."
In August, DHS launched its own inquiry to identify noncitizens on state voter lists.
A federal whistleblower statement alleged the initiative was hurried, prone to errors, and potentially unlawful, though DHS defended its actions as being conducted "diligently and professionally."
The effort to establish a centralized voter database forms part of broader measures taken during Trump's second term to reshape federal election administration.
Most attempts have been blocked by lower courts, as the Constitution delegates election regulation to the states and Congress rather than the president.
In mid-September, the Supreme Court turned down a separate attempt by Trump to restrict mail-in voting procedures prior to the midterms.
Research shows that noncitizen voting, which is already illegal and carries felony penalties including deportation, is exceptionally rare. Nevertheless, Trump has remained fixated on the claim that large numbers of noncitizens are casting ballots in American elections.

articles.title_orig: Wisconsin frat leaders arrested after 30 pledges found in filthy basement, injured and covered in condiments
articles.title_zh: Wisconsin frat leaders arrested after 30 pledges found in filthy basement, injured and covered in condiments
articles.content_orig:
Two leaders of an underground University of Wisconsin-Madison fraternity were arrested and charged with hazing after dozens of pledges were found injured, shirtless and covered in condiments in a sweltering basement.
The Madison Police Department said Thursday it received an anonymous tip about an event in the basement of an off-campus chapter house.
Alpha Epsilon Pi was kicked off campus as a recognized chapter in 2015, but the organization maintained a presence at the Madison home.
Police say about 30 pledges, most of whom were 18, were found partially-clothed in a filthy basement around 8:20 p.m. on Wednesday.
The apparent hazing victims were “covered in food, condiments, and other liquids” and “had visible injuries consistent with being physically assaulted.” The thermostat was set to 81 degrees, making the basement hot and humid, police said.
Brayden Klein and Samuel Vane, both 20, were charged with hazing and disorderly conduct. Madison police are still investigating the matter.
Klein and Vane each posted $400 bail around 1 a.m. on Thursday morning and were released from the Dane County Jail, officials confirmed. It was not immediately clear when they must appear in court to face the charges.
Klein and Vane could not immediately be reached by NBC News for comment.
The university said in a statement that while it stopped recognizing Alpha Epsilon Pi about a decade ago, the national organization has continued to recognize the Madison chapter, allowing it to exist in the community.
The University of Wisconsin-Madison said in a statement that it will investigate students “implicated in the incident.”
Alpha Epsilon Pi was founded as a Jewish fraternity in 1913.
The national organization’s website lists a Madison, Wisconsin, chapter called “Pi,” but it does not cite an affiliation with the university.
In a statement, the national fraternity said it is taking the allegations “extremely seriously” and said it would “cooperate fully with the authorities investigating this matter.”
“Any member found responsible for criminal conduct in this matter will be expelled from AEPi, and we will support prosecution to the fullest extent of the law,” the statement said. “We will also work with the university in hopes that they will take action against individual perpetrators for violation of the student code of conduct.”
“Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for ... Anyone who engages in hazing forfeits the privilege of being an AEPi brother,” the statement continued.
Anti-hazing advocates say underground chapters present a unique risk for hazing incidents because they are not monitored by officials at their college or university.
There have been almost 130 hazing-related deaths with an average of five per year in the U.S. since 2000, according to HazingInfo.org, a research and advocacy website that tracks incidents.
Shayna Jacobs is a national reporter for NBC News digital.

Published: 01:42 EDT, 25 September 2026 | Updated: 08:50 EDT, 25 September 2026
Donald Trump pulled out all the stops for his glamorous State Dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping as the two spent much of his visit discussing the toughest issues facing their nations.
The lavish black-tie affair in the historic East Room stands as one of the most star-studded evenings of the administration, offering a glitzy opportunity to smooth over notoriously fierce geopolitical friction with the superpower.
Trump heaped praise on Xi, whom he says he has developed a 'truly great friendship' with over his decade in politics .
However, the two nations remain divided on the war in Iran and are still grappling to find common ground on trade and how to best navigate the jarring advances of artificial intelligence .
During talks with Xi in Washington ahead of the dinner, the two sides discussed the Iran War, according to state broadcaster China Central Television.
Trump has argued to little effect that Beijing , which is far more dependent on Gulf oil than the US, has plenty of incentive to use its sway with Tehran to help force an end to the conflict.
But the President's war of choice has unnerved China, with the government condemning American and Israeli military action and Xi previously expressing concerns that the conflict signaled a return to what he called the 'law of the jungle.'
The US administration has warned the country, which is Tehran's biggest trading partner, not to aid Iran's military effort.

Xi, during Thursday's talks, said China supports the US and Iran returning to a short-lived interim deal from the summer to wind down the war, according to CCTV.
That agreement broke down soon after it was signed in June as the countries traded renewed fire over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for energy shipments.
The pair also discussed artificial intelligence - or 'superintelligence' as Trump wants to rebrand it - as the dinner saw key figures from the field in attendance.
The President has been dismissive of calls for greater regulation amid growing global anxiety that the technology will kill jobs or potentially even wipe out humanity.
'I want to leave it exactly where it is,' Trump wrote. 'That is China's position also.'
But Xi, in his opening comments, said that the two countries had 'the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.'
The two countries' finance ministers met earlier this week, with the US proposing a new 'notification mechanism' for AI incidents between the two nations.
During their private conversation on Thursday, Xi told Trump he hopes America can adhere to opposing Taiwan independence and urged him to 'prudently handle the Taiwan issue,' according to the Chinese state media outlet Xinhua.

The White House did not immediately release any readout of the talks and Trump, who frequently offers his own take of his interactions with foreign leaders on his social media platform, has yet to weigh in on the substance of his conversations with Xi.
Trump, who is in the midst of a legal fight after trying to bar CNN, MSNOW, and Politico from the White House, did complain that TV networks 'refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years .'
The White House's five-network television pool rotation refused to cover Trump's events in response to the action against CNN.
China has made clear it views Taiwan as the most sensitive issue in the US-China relationship.
Beijing considers the island to be Chinese territory and vows to annex it by force if necessary. The United States is obligated by law to provide Taiwan with sufficient hardware to deter any armed attack from the mainland.
The US has said it opposes any unilateral changes to the status quo by either side.
China has repeatedly pressed Washington to permanently halt the arms sales, including when Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May.
After that meeting, Trump said he was holding off on final approval for a record $14 billion arms package that was in the pipeline.

Trump had made clear he wanted to impress Xi with the visit.
The Republican President made sure construction of a new helicopter landing pad on the White House’s South Lawn was completed before the visit and he met Xi and his wife on Wednesday evening when they flew into Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
Trump took the podium to kick off the grand evening.
‘You are truly outstanding, amazing people… we hope to show you the same honor as you return to Washington for the first time in over a decade,’ the President started in his speech.
'As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure and we have never gotten along better.'
Trump invited guests to take a look at his new ballroom, which he lamented was not ready in time for their dinner.

articles.title_orig: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
articles.title_zh: Susan Sarandon and Hannah Einbinder arrested at anti-Netanyahu protest in New York
articles.content_orig:
Actors detained at Jewish Voice for Peace demonstration against Israeli prime minister’s address to the UN general assembly
Oscar-winning actor Susan Sarandon and Hacks star Hannah Einbinder were among people detained by police in New York on Thursday as they moved in to break up a protest against Benjamin Netanyahu .
Agence France-Presse footage shows NYPD officers cuffing Thelma & Louise star Sarandon at the demo in the city as the Israeli prime minister was readying to address the United Nations general assembly.
The New York Post reported Einbinder had also been marched away from the demonstration organised by Jewish Voice for Peace, where protesters held banners that read “Stop Arming Israel” and “End the Genocide.”
A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an “unscheduled demonstration” where people were blocking an intersection.
“Members of the NYPD Community Affairs Bureau issued … warnings, advising participants that they should leave,” the spokesperson said.
“They continued to block the intersection. Multiple individuals who didn’t comply were taken into custody,” she said, without providing the number of people arrested.
Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York ⁠City council member Chi Ossé were also among those arrested.
Inside the general assembly, dozens of envoys from across the world walked out as Netanyahu began his speech, where he assailed both enemies and allies that have crossed him in recent months, including Britain and France, which have recently moved to recognise the state of Palestine.
“They accuse Israel , tiny Israel, of colonialism – some colonialism. And who’s accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God’s sakes, they invented the term,” he told the assembly.
Sarandon, whose movie hits also include The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Dead Man Walking and The Witches of Eastwick, is no stranger to protests over Israel’s war in Gaza.
The US actor told journalists at the Venice film festival this month she was losing work because of her outspoken views.
“I’ve still had movies taken away recently because there are agencies that are telling people not to hire me still. But that’s the power structure,” she said.
“I think there has been a change in terms of the understanding of the situation and the general public, but there are still very strongly held positions within my industry that are held by Zionists and who have not relaxed their feelings towards me.
“But I found my family, I found my people, and I’m OK,” she added.
Einbinder has previously said the cost of not speaking up about Palestine is greater than losing her Hollywood career, citing industry backlash to actors such as Sarandon and Melissa Barrera .
“I think what they know is what I know, which is that the cost of not speaking is higher,” she told Cannes film festival earlier this year.
“There is a greater toll in not speaking and you’ve just got to have your priorities straight. I am under no impression that my small career could ever measure up in comparison to even one human life. It’s an obligation and I will always do it.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Embattled New Jersey Lt. Governor Resigns After Ethics Inquiry
articles.title_zh: Embattled New Jersey Lt. Governor Resigns After Ethics Inquiry
articles.content_orig:
Multiple New Jersey leaders had called for his resignation.
Dale Caldwell resigned Friday as lieutenant governor of New Jersey after an investigation found "serious, repeated violations of state policy, including ethical lapses and a substantiated finding of sexual harassment," Gov. Mikie Sherrill said.
His resignation came after the governor released on Thursday the findings of an investigation into Caldwell over multiple ethics violation complaints.
The probe found there was credible evidence that Caldwell made "a romantic advance toward a female staffer's friend," and after his advance was rebuffed, he made sexually inappropriate comments to the staffer about their friend, according to the investigation's findings.
The investigation "lays out a pattern and practice of long term concerning behavior multiple ethics trainings, multiple ethics violations, sexual harassment, substantial claims of sexual harassment and statements by the lieutenant governor in the report so obviously he was fully involved in this as well," Sherrill said at a news conference Friday.
In a statement to ABC New York station WABC, Caldwell's attorney said they will "continue to forcefully challenge the report."
"Dr. Caldwell's resignation, submitted to put an end to the targeted campaign to discredit his character, does not in any way diminish our outrage concerning the investigative process and its specious findings," said Thomas R. Calcagni, counsel to Caldwell. "Counsel is fully exploring all legal remedies to ensure a true, balanced, and unbiased record."
The probe began with an anonymous complaint accusing the lieutenant governor of "hitting on women at functions while traveling using taxpayer money," and "handing out his state business cards and asking women out on dates," according to investigators.
Caldwell's team "repeatedly cautioned him about his behavior," investigators said, but they found he also tried "on multiple occasions to secure a promotion for a state employee with whom he had a romantic relationship."
"I hold everyone in my Administration to the highest ethical standard. We all have a duty to follow our state ethics and harassment policy and our Code of Conduct. Anyone who violates these will be held accountable," Sherrill said in a statement Thursday where she gave Caldwell a day to resign.
Several other prominent New Jersey elected officials, including Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., also called on Caldwell to resign after the report was released.
"New Jerseyans deserve to have public servants who work to earn and keep their trust, not undermine it. The findings of the independent report are unacceptable," Kim said in a social media post Friday.
In New Jersey, the lieutenant governor serves as the secretary of state as well and oversees the state agency that includes oversight of elections. New Jersey's counties and municipalities handle much of the administration of elections.
Sherrill said Friday she is appointing an interim secretary of state to oversee the midterm elections.
-ABC News' Ivan Pereira contributed to this report.

New Jersey Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell — Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s handpicked No. 2 she once lauded as a “voice for the voiceless” — has resigned under the weight of a growing sexual harassment scandal that led to his boss calling for his ouster.
The first-term governor said Caldwell submitted his resignation Friday afternoon, a day after she publicly called on him to step down after an investigation substantiated claims of sexual harassment and “serious repeated violations of state policy, including ethical lapses.”
Caldwell, the former president of Centenary University, was accused of making sexual comments to an aide and using his position to try to score a promotion for his girlfriend.
But in a defiant interview, the embattled pol denied he was resigning over his scandalous behavior.
“I’m not resigning because of the report,” Caldwell told the New York Times . “It’s false. I’m resigning because I don’t want to be a distraction to the administration.”
“I’m supportive of the Sherrill administration,” he added. “I want her to be as successful as possible.”
Sherrill formally called for Caldwell’s resignation in a statement Thursday night, the same day an explosive 61-page ethics report detailing his creepy conduct was released, and gave him 24 hours to step down.
“I hold everyone in my Administration to the highest ethical standard. We all have a duty to follow our state ethics and harassment policy and our Code of Conduct. Anyone who violates these will be held accountable.”
Caldwell, 66, blamed race as a driving force behind the investigation, which was sparked by an anonymous complaint in May.
“Unfortunately, in this current political environment, false accusations, especially against people of color, seem to be commonplace,” he said at the time.
Caldwell’s shocking fall from grace stands in stark contrast to the high praise Sherrill heaped upon him during her run for governor.
In July 2025, Sherrill called him a “voice for the voiceless,” and someone who is “committed to New Jersey” when she tapped him to be her running mate against Republican Jack Ciattarelli.
“I’m proud to select Dale Caldwell as my Lieutenant Governor running mate because we share a commitment to public service and challenging the status quo,” Sherrill said at the time, lauding him for marching in Selma, Ala. with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
The voluminous report, based on a probe led by former New Jersey Attorney General Christopher Porrino, highlights egregious examples of Caldwell abusing his position including scoring pricey tickets for romantic conquests, securing his girlfriend a cushy state promotion and tasking his aides with finding him a “first lady.”
The disgraced lieutenant governor brought one or more guests to seven ticketed events without paying for them between Feb. 19 and May 23 — including at the State Opera of New Jersey and a Rowan University Rosa Parks Scholarship Luncheon. Tickets ranged from $65 to $300, the report said.
One of the worst accusations featured in the report occurred in April, when Caldwell, 66, hit on a staffer’s much-younger friend at an official event, then threw a tantrum in the back of his state vehicle after his advances were rejected, allegedly telling the aide, “you young women are looking for young sperm.”
Caldwell’s attorney, Thomas Calcagni, denied that his client made the stomach-churning comment.
Caldwell, a divorced Methodist pastor, allegedly tasked a staffer with finding him a “first lady,” and when she said no, he became “pushy” on the subject, the report said.
Sherrill was barred from firing Caldwell — only the state Legislature can remove lieutenant governors through impeachment.

articles.title_zh: Global Citizen Festival canceled as powerful nor'easter expected to slam NYC through the weekend
articles.content_orig:
Millions of Americans are gearing up for a rare, multiday nor’easter that is set to start pummeling the Northeast with rain, wind and flooding Friday.
Coastal flood alerts are in effect for 33 million people along the East Coast as of Friday morning, affecting states from Virginia to Rhode Island.
The storm already brought gusty winds and early flooding across the Eastern Seaboard on Thursday, with rough waves pounding shorelines. Winds up to 65 mph are forecast, with the strongest winds expected through Saturday night on Long Island in New York and in New England.
Heavy rain bands — up to 4 to 6 inches — will hit the area Saturday and into Sunday, and winds will push water onto shore, with 1 to 4 feet of inundation expected.
Widespread 1 to 3 inches of rain is possible from the Interstate 95 corridor to the coast. The Jersey Shore, Long Island and coastal New England are the locations likely to see the highest rain totals.
Waves of 10 to 18 feet are expected, with coastal flooding forecasts of 1 to 4 feet depending on the area.
The system is expected to intensify as it moves north. It will come onshore around New Jersey.
On Friday, the nor’easter will intensify as onshore winds increase from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina, to Cape Cod, Massachusetts. By Saturday, rain will begin from the Jersey Shore to eastern Massachusetts and is expected to last all day.
Saturday will also feature the highest wind potential, with wind gusts that could reach 60 mph in coastal locations.
Rain will continue for the Northeast and New England on Sunday, as beaches continue to take a beating from the strong onshore winds.
The storm will still be spinning just off the coast Monday. While winds will be weaker, rain and beach erosion will continue.
Winds are expected to lead to travel delays and power outages into Monday.
Southeast New England faces the highest risk of power outages because of the strongest wind potential and top-heavy trees with leaves still on them.
As of Friday afternoon, before the rain started in some areas, three major music events set for this weekend had already been canceled, including the annual Global Citizen Festival held at Central Park in New York City.
“Due to the extreme weather forecast for New York City this weekend, we have made the difficult decision, in consultation with the City of New York and NYC Parks, to cancel this year’s Global Citizen Festival,” the organization wrote on social media .
“Safety has to come first,” Global Citizen added, noting that this is the first time the festival has been canceled in 14 years.
All Things Go , another festival that was being held at Forrest Hills Stadium in Queens this weekend, was also canceled due to the weather.
And Ed Sheeran had to cancel his Boston shows , scheduled for Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium, Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement.
Areas of New Jersey were already lashed by rough surf Friday morning, with videos showing waves crashing along the shore.
“The waves, the wave actions, the way it comes in, it just takes everything in its path,” said Mike Jones, the emergency management director for Upper Township, New Jersey. “And there’s really no way to stop Mother Nature.”
A full moon Saturday night is also expected to lift tides up to 5 to 6 inches.
One New Jersey resident told NBC News that to prepare for this weekend’s nor’easter, she closed up her whole house.
Outside Washington, abnormally high tides were seen along the Potomac River, inundating roads with floodwaters and leaving a popular Maryland music festival practically underwater. The first day of events was canceled in advance.
In North Carolina, winds greater than 50 mph have been recorded. A video showed a car in the state nearly swept into the ocean before a tow truck saved it.
Elsewhere in the region, emergency preparedness crews are cutting down trees and readying sandbags. Officials have warned of flooding in neighborhoods.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo is barreling toward Hawaii with 80 mph winds. It is a Category 1 storm and is moving north at 5 mph. At some point over the weekend, it is expected to become a major hurricane, upgraded to a Category 3 or 4.
The storm is forecast to stay south of Hawaii, but the islands will still feel Nolo’s wrath. Heavy rainfall — up to 30 inches on the Big Island — and intense winds are already affecting the state. People in Hawaii are preparing for the worst, expecting catastrophic flooding.
Just last month, Hurricane Lala brought destruction to Hawaii’s Big Island, damaging more than 100 homes and stranding people without water and power.
In addition to dangerous surf and damaging winds, mudslides are a major concern in Hawaii.
As of Thursday night, stores were sold out of generators and gas cans. Shops were boarded up and blocked with sandbags. Schools were let out Thursday to give residents more time to prepare for the storm’s effects.
Nolo is expected to reach full strength sometime Friday night.

articles.title_orig: New report: Utah Valley University tried to warn Charlie Kirk’s staff of risks, but team ignored concerns
articles.title_zh: New report: Utah Valley University tried to warn Charlie Kirk’s staff of risks, but team ignored concerns
articles.content_orig:
According to report, school staff recommended event move to a more secure location weeks before Kirk was fatally shot
A new report says that Turning Point USA insisted the conservative political group’s leader Charlie Kirk speak outdoors at Utah Valley University – where he was ultimately assassinated – despite security concerns raised with his team by the school’s leaders and its police chief.
The independent report with those findings was commissioned by UVU and released on Friday. The report examined security procedures leading up to the 31-year-old’s fatal shooting on 10 September 2025 during a talk at the university’s campus in Orem, Utah.
According to the 158-page report, school staff recommended Turning Point USA (TPUSA) move its event to a more secure location weeks before Kirk’s slaying. However, TPUSA “insisted upon” an outdoor location which “created significant protective operations considerations”, the report said.
It added that a face-to-face, pre-event briefing and walkthrough with UVU police chief Jeff Long and the TPUSA protection detail – including the organization’s security supervisor Dan Flood – “should also have occurred” on UVU’s campus hours prior to the event.
“Chief Long texted Dan Flood to meet on the Hall of Flags outdoor pedestrian walkway at 11[am], however, this face-to-face meeting did not occur,” the report said.
Kirk was shot and killed by a sniper that day in the early afternoon.
According to the report, the university also asked TPUSA for an estimated attendance figure. But the organization never provided one, despite saying it would control ticketing for the event, Utah’s Salt Lake Tribune newspaper reported .
“Based on our review of all available information, that at no time during the events leading up to the assassination of Charlie Kirk, or in its aftermath, did any employee or agent of UVU act in bad faith or in willful and wanton disregard for the safety of others,” the report said.
However, it also noted UVU’s having deferred to TPUSA on various event logistics. “Several key event security decisions were deferred to the TPUSA field representative even though UVU staff members raised concerns, including concerns related to holding the event in the outdoor fountain courtyard area and using TPUSA’s ticketing process,” the university’s report said.
“Those decisions placed the event in an area that was more difficult to control and limited UVU’s ability to obtain reliable, real-time information regarding anticipated attendance and crowd size.”
The report added: “UVU should have retained decision-making authority over key security-related issues, including venue selection, ticketing, access control and other conditions necessary to support campus safety.”
In response to the report, Kirk family attorney Brett Parkinson said: “UVU hosted this event, and in doing so, assumed responsibility for the safety of all in attendance, including Charlie. The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement.
“Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU’s fatal shortcomings that day.”
Meanwhile, a statement from Jon Anderson, UVU’s president, said the university had a responsibility to “learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations”.
“This requires humility, an honest examination of our policies and practices, and a commitment to act on what we learn,” Anderson’s statement also said.
Anderson, who became the university’s president in August, also said in his statement that UVU had made “meaningful progress in strengthening campus safety over the past year”.
Kirk’s family is planning to sue the university. His family alleged in a 16 September legal notice presaging wrongful death litigation that UVU had placed “a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event … surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms” – and that the setup was like “walking him into a fishbowl”.
UVU said it was aware of the notice and said it “addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes”, according to the Tribune.
Utah resident Tyler Robinson has been charged with aggravated murder in connection with Kirk’s killing. He has pleaded not guilty, and no trial date had been set for him as of Friday.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday after a federal judge ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore their press access.
The re-entry came after a chaotic morning, during which the three outlets filed an emergency request for a hearing, accusing the Trump Administration of having “repeatedly violated” the court order and refusing several reporters access to the White House grounds. "This morning, journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in the court document.
Judge Timothy Kelly had given the Trump Administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond to the outlets' filing.
In a court filing of its own, the White House said it "began the process" of reinstating press badges shortly at 7:25 a.m. ET and laid out a timeline of what followed. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Early Thursday, in a District of Columbia court, Judge Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” He ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ​ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning .
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge over the ban and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted : “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
“Either the preliminary injunction will be issued or denied,” says Eugene Volokh, a law professor at UCLA who specializes in the First Amendment. “The temporary restraining order would then lapse, and whichever side loses can then appeal to the D.C. Circuit.”
Instead of an appeal, Trump could file for emergency relief from the D.C. court, similar to how CNN, MS NOW, and Politico did Thursday, according to experts.
But “emergency relief is usually harder to get than a resolution through appeal,” says Volokh.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.
Volokh says that legal precedent in the D.C. Circuit, used in both the ongoing case and that of Acosta, has “already been set” for areas of the White House usually open to the media, including the press briefing room.
“The government can't exclude reporters based on viewpoint, and cannot take away a press pass without due process, without some sort of hearing opportunity to be heard, an explanation of what it is that they supposedly did wrong, what rules they violated,” he says.
In light of this, an appeal from the Trump Administration after a preliminary injunction would likely be rejected in the D.C. Circuit, he argues. However, the President may find a better chance in the Supreme Court.
“Generally speaking, the First Amendment does not secure a right of access to government office buildings,” says Volokh, once again noting the exception of areas usually granted access for press. "The same position could be taken by the Supreme Court, and [it] might say: 'Look, the government can pick and choose whom to allow on its property,'" he says.
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said : “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post —announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.

They also visited the National Archives in Washington, DC.
• This was Xi and Trump’s second summit this year , and the Chinese leader’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade, as they try to manage the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship .
• On Thursday, Trump hosted a state dinner at the White House. Top US tech executives , including Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, were seen at the event.
• The two leaders underlined the importance of discussions on AI. Other issues on trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran also loomed large.
Our live coverage of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s state visit with US President Donald Trump has ended. Read analysis on the Xi-Trump meeting here .
Chinese leader Xi Jinping returned to the White House this morning, where he and his wife, Peng Liyuan, met US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump for tea.
After a visit to the National Archives, Xi wrapped his three-day summit with Trump. He’s now on a plane bound for Beijing.

Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, arrived to Joint Base Andrews for their red carpet departure after a visit to the National Archives with the president and first lady Melania Trump.
President Donald Trump hosted China’s leader Xi Jinping Friday at a site that is home to some of the nation’s most consequential founding documents, offering the autocratic leader a symbolic display of democracy.
Inside the grand rotunda of the National Archives, Trump and Xi, joined by their spouses and translators, viewed the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution. Honoring the United States’ 250th anniversary, the documents underscored the nation’s founding ideals, providing some contrast with China — which is under an authoritarian, one-party system — even as the leaders showcased warm, friendly relations throughout the visit.
Trump stopped to speak with reporters assembled inside the rotunda multiple times, including fielding a question from a CNN reporter who was serving as the network TV pool representative, one day after reporters from three outlets had their White House credentials restored.
And Trump, a real estate developer who has embroiled himself in a series of construction projects at the White House and across Washington, DC, also admired the building.
“This is when they built it properly,” he said as he inspected the 75-foot ceiling of the building, completed in 1935.
President Donald Trump said Friday that he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed the war in Iran at their meeting at the White House.
“We did,” Trump said in response to a question from CNN, during his tour with Xi at the National Archives.
When asked if he and Xi made progress on the Strait of Hormuz, where slowed traffic due to the war has drastically increased global energy costs, Trump responded: “I think we’re going to do great.”
China’s leader Xi Jinping looked ahead to upcoming visits with US President Donald Trump, underscoring the warm — and consequential — relationship between the two leaders on display throughout the three-day state visit.
“The prospects for this relationship” will get “brighter,” Xi said during a tea with the Trumps at the White House, according to a translation.
He continued, “Looking ahead to the remainder of this year, there will be two more opportunities for us to meet each other. Firstly, the APEC meeting in China and then the G20 summit in the United States.”
The Chinese leader went on to say he would “welcome” the president and first lady back to China.
The president appeared to confirm he would be in attendance.
“Thank you very much. We will, and we’ll be speaking a lot,” Trump said.
Trump confirmed in a subsequent post to social media that he planned to attend the APEC summit, which will be hosted in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump is hosting the G20 Summit in Miami in December.
Xi’s trip to Washington marks the second time the leaders have convened this year and the third in Trump’s second term in office.

“I think our farmers are going to be very happy,” Trump said ahead of a tea meeting with Xi at the White House. “A lot of very positive things happened, but America is very happy about this visit and I’m sure China is very happy also.”
The president’s remarks came at the outset of the second day of Xi’s visit, with the two slated later on Friday to visit the National Archives. Neither Trump nor Xi have publicly discussed any potential new agreements between the two nations, even as both framed the visit as a success.
“We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries,” Trump said.
During the tea service in the White House’s Red Room, the president and first lady Melania Trump gifted Xi and Madam Peng Liyuan a photo album with pictures from the state visit.
